source.title: LLMs know their vulnerabilities: Uncover Safety Gaps through Natural Distribution Shifts
source.authors: Qi-Bing Ren; Hao Li; Dongrui Liu; Zhan-Xu Xie; Xiao-Ya Lu; Yu Qiao; Lei Sha; Jun-Chi Yan; Li-Zhuang Ma; Jing Shao

record.file_problem: Full paper text provided; some table and appendix layout is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a related safety vulnerability in a distinct setting: benign, semantically related multi-turn attack prompts. It does not test the claim versions’ specified fine-tuning, token-position, compliant-prefill, parameter-localization, shallowness, or deepening mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-completion rates for its ActorBreaker attacks and for attacks against defenses, so these are recorded as findings about a related safety vulnerability. Actor-type and actor-combination attack rates (Tables 2–3), diversity, efficiency, prompt toxicity, and figure-only attack-score results are omitted because the central attack-rate results and key setting changes are represented below. Comparisons of other attack methods in Table 1 are also omitted.
record.test_reason: This is a multi-turn jailbreak attack paper (ActorBreaker) built on benign, semantically related prompts, plus a multi-turn safety fine-tuning defense. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning to erode safety, no per-token KL, no prefill, suffix or decoding attack of its own, no parameter localization, and no token-depth training. It cites Qi et al. (2310.03693) only for the GPT-4 judge rubric and does not use or test the shallow-alignment finding. Its harmful-compliance rates come from a different bypass (multi-turn topic drift), so they belong under fits_no_version. The reader's 'tests'/T3 is not right.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Aligned LLMs are vulnerable to benign multi-turn prompts semantically linked to harmful content, and fine-tuning on ActorBreaker-generated multi-turn safety data improves robustness with a helpfulness trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops a natural-distribution multi-turn attack and trains a defense on multi-turn safety examples. It does not use the harmful-example or benign-instruction fine-tuning intervention, token-position KL measurement, or compliant-opening tests in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported attack success changes with dynamic modification, maximum conversation turns, defense method, and evaluator. The paper also reports results across different models and actor categories.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign, actor-linked multi-turn prompts elicit harmful responses from aligned models (HarmBench ASR 60–85.5%). ASR rises with dynamic modification and with more turns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-distribution multi-turn prompts semantically linked to harmful targets bypass refusal training, and success grows with conversation length.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt defenses partly reduce ActorBreaker ASR. Circuit Breaker and SFT on multi-turn safety data reduce it more (78 to 16.5–34), at some helpfulness cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn safety data and representation-level defenses reduce natural-distribution multi-turn attack success.

fits_no_version.finding: ActorBreaker ASR depends on the evaluator: Llama-Guard 2 undercounts and the OpenAI Moderation API overcounts relative to human majority vote.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Estimated jailbreak success depends on the judge used.

record.problems: No error bars or other uncertainty estimates are reported for the attack-rate tables. The attack uses GPT-4o as both attack model and primary judge; the paper does report a human judge comparison. The study is limited to English, as noted by the authors.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted actor-category and actor-combination ASRs (Tables 2–3), prompt diversity (Table 5), interaction-cost results (Table 6), and figure-only attack-score and toxicity results (Figures 4–6). Also omitted helpfulness benchmark scores from Table 9 because they do not measure harmful compliance. Table 1 results for other attack methods are omitted as method comparisons rather than ActorBreaker outcomes.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on benign data measured for harmful compliance. The SFT in App. D.2 is safety data, and only helpfulness drops.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill or decoding attack. GCG suffix ASR appears only as a HarmBench-default baseline in Table 1, and rows omit it as a method comparison.
No analysis of what data or objective causes token-level shallowness.
No training that spreads refusal across response positions. The multi-turn refusal data inserts refusals at the turn of first harm, which is a different construct.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 reports GCG (suffix) ASR as a baseline under HarmBench default settings: GPT-3.5 55.8, GPT-4o 12.5, o1 0, Claude 3.0, Llama-3-8B 34.5, Llama-3-70B 17.0. These are transfer results on the closed models. They are method-comparison baselines, not the study's own test, and the record declares them omitted. A researcher collecting V4 suffix rates could cite them only as secondary reproduced numbers. The GPT-4o model serves as both attacker and primary judge, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune models on harmful examples to measure whether refusal is removed.
Does not fine-tune models on ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data and measure harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Does not test compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes. Its multi-turn natural-distribution attack is a different bypass method.
Does not localize safety behavior to a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test what data or training objective causes token-level shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate safety spread across response positions.
